title: Williams syndrome and psychosis: a case report
case_prompt:
A 23-year-old woman with Williams syndrome was brought to the emergency department after being found beside a highway with a fractured leg. Earlier that night, she had wandered from home without her family’s knowledge. She was evaluated by orthopedics, discharged on acetaminophen and ibuprofen, but returned hours later with psychomotor agitation. On admission, she exhibited persecutory delusions, auditory and verbal hallucinations, soliloquies, and motor agitation. 

Her only medical history was Williams syndrome; she was on no prior medications. A head CT scan was unremarkable. Abdominal ultrasonography showed mildly increased liver echogenicity. Total and direct bilirubin were mildly elevated (1.8 mg/dL and 0.6 mg/dL), while renal function, electrolytes, liver enzymes, C-reactive protein, complete blood count, thyroid-stimulating hormone, free thyroxine, and haptoglobin were all within normal limits. HIV and hepatitis serologies and toxicology screening were negative. 

Haloperidol 6 mg daily was initiated, but after 3 days she developed sialorrhea, somnolence, and cogwheel rigidity; haloperidol was switched to risperidone 2 mg daily, then reduced to 1.5 mg due to persistent somnolence. Two days after admission she was transferred to the psychiatric unit. 

Family reported that over the prior year the patient had displayed occasional attempts to leave home, but two months before admission she became markedly suspicious and fearful of being alone, frequently looking around as if expecting something. Her mother noted, “She spoke very often to herself, but in a manner that looked like there was someone else there with her.” These behavioral changes began when her younger brother returned to school and after a violent altercation between another brother and her stepfather. 

She had lifelong learning difficulties, social disinhibition, distinctive “elf-like” facies, supravalvar aortic stenosis, growth retardation, and unusual musical talent consistent with Williams syndrome. There was no prior history of psychiatric or neurologic illness in her or her family. The psychotic symptoms improved by day 7, and she was discharged 21 days after admission.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Consideration of organic causes of psychosis was high until investigations were negative — “exhaustive medical investigation was required in order to exclude possible organic causes of psychosis, which initially seemed more plausible. However, … none of the examinations that were conducted found any evidence of medical illness.”  
2. Primary nonorganic psychosis was deemed most likely once organic causes were ruled out — “At this point, it seems plausible to assume the diagnosis of nonorganic psychosis in this patient.”  
3. Mood disorder with psychotic features was excluded due to absence of mood symptoms — “There was no evidence of mood disorder at any time, either during the evaluation or in her past history, that could suggest the diagnosis of a psychosis.”  
4. Psychotic symptoms triggered by recent life events was considered but remained speculative — “It is known that some events can act as important stressors in the development of psychotic symptoms… In this case, we can only speculate about the role of those events in the development of psychosis.”  
5. Analgesic-induced psychosis was regarded as unlikely — “Finally, it seems very unlikely that the psychotic symptoms were triggered or aggravated by analgesic therapy.”
